Mayor Rios called the meeting to order at 6:04 p.m. in the Council Chambers, Norwalk

CITY COUNCIL COMMENTS

City Council thanked the and Recreation and Park Services department for a successful
Egg-Stravagant Egg Hunt. Vice Mayor Ayala requested the City conduct outreach
regarding Community Development Block Grant Funding for roof repairs to assist senior
residents. Councilmember Perez shared that City newsletters were distributed;
highlighted the Public Safety department for keeping residents updated on current
weather conditions; reported on her attendance at the State of the College Luncheon and
Los Angeles County Advocacy Day. Councilmember Valencia reported on her
attendance at Disney’s Beauty and the Beast Junior Musical at Benton Middle School;
thanked Theresa Devoy, City Clerk, for assisting her with her Fair Political Practice
Commission forms; and shared that Congresswoman Linda Sanchez submitted a check
to the City in the amount of $2.1 million dollars, which will be used for water system and
Norwalk Transportation bus stop improvements. Councilmember Ramirez recognized
commissioners in attendance; reported on his attendance at the Los Angeles Sanitation
District Nos. 2 and 18 meetings and 91 Interstate 605 Corridor Cities Joint Power
Authority meeting; and thanked staff for focusing efforts on the Interstate 105 /Studebaker
area and requested they put more pressure on Caltrans to address concerns. Mayor
Rios reported on her attendance at the Mayors and City Managers Roundtable; invited
all to attend Vista Verde Park Playground Ribbon Cutting Ceremony on April 8, Friends
of the Norwalk Library Fundraiser at So Cal Pizza on April 9, and the Mayor’s Prayer
Breakfast at the Double Tree on April 17; shared that correspondence was sent to Los
Angeles County Assembly Member, Supervisor, and Senator regarding the safety
concerns of the Interstate 105 /Studebaker area, and she held an interview with the media
to further discuss the issues.

SUBJECT:  RESOLUTION NO. 24-16 – BUDGET AMENDMENT – RESIDENTIAL
  REHABILITATION PROGRAM

Background:

On October 3, 2023, the City Council approved a substantial amendment to the Fiscal Year (FY)
2023/24 Annual Action Plan to reallocate unused Community Development Block Grant (CDBG)
funds in the amount of $615,267 to the Capital Improvement Program (CIP), and allocate
$600,000 from General Fund for a new citywide Residential Rehabilitation Program (Program).
Prior to this amendment, CDBG funds were allocated for the Home Improvement Program,
although due to strict guidelines, a limited number of people were served. The reallocation of
CDBG funding to the CIP program funded much needed repairs to streets, sidewalks, curbs,
gutters, and Americans with Disabilities Act access ramps.

Staff completed development of the new Program that is ready to be implemented. It will initially
serve residents on the waitlist for the CDBG Home Improvement Program. Once all applicants
on the waitlist have been assisted, staff will assess if additional residents can be assisted through
the Program. The program funding will be allocated into the following categories:

  •  Accessibility upgrades: $100,000
  •  Air conditioning / cooling units: $100,000
  •  Home safety inspections / repairs: $100,000
  •  Senior Roof Repair / Replacement: $100,000
  •  Sustainability / energy efficient repairs: $100,000
  •  Administrative costs: $100,000

SUBJECT:  RENEWAL OF GENERAL SERVICES AGREEMENT

Background:

The current General Services Agreement (GSA) between the City and the County of Los Angeles
(County) was approved June 1, 2019 and scheduled to expire on June 30, 2024.

The GSA enables cities and other public entities to receive miscellaneous services from the
County on an “as-needed” basis. These services can include such functions as predatory animal
control, prosecution of city ordinances, direct assessment collection, and a variety of public
works activities. The agreement places the City under no obligation but does provide the
necessary means to request any needed contract services. Specific and ongoing services, such
as law enforcement Los Angeles County Sheriff Department (LASD) are handled separately by
the responsible County departments through individual service agreements.

  The City of Los Angeles contracts with the Departments of Beaches & Harbors and Fire for maintenance and lifeguard services for four beaches located within the city through a Joint Powers Agreement (JPA) with the County.

  The Fire Department provides beach lifeguard services to the City of El Segundo through a contract with Chevron.
4
  The Internal Services Department (ISD) provides IT services (mainframe access) for the City of Los Angeles and the City of Long Beach. IT services (eGis services) are provided to the following cities: Arcadia, Hawthorne, Redondo Beach, Santa Monica and Torrance and radio telecommunications services (CWIRS) to all 88 cities. ISD Fleet
section provides fuel to San Bernardino County's Public Works department and the City of La Puente for the LASD Sheriff Station. ISD provides Mail Services to the City Halls of the City of Los Angeles and the City of Long Beach. ISD Power Plant provides chilled water for the A/C unit and heat for the Santa Clarita Library. ISD also provides the Santa Clarita Library testing for the irrigation backflow.

  The Department of Mental Health (DMH) contracts with the City of Gardena to provide socialization services.

  DMH entered into a MOA with the Cities of Alhambra, Azusa, Bell, Bell Gardens, Covina, Culver City, Downey, Glendora, Huntington Park, Montebello, Monterey Park, Signal Hill, South Gate, Vernon, and West Covina police departments to develop mental health evaluation team and co-response models.
7
  DMH entered into a partnership through a Memorandum of Cooperative Agreement with the City of Burbank to develop a mental health evaluation team and one FTE psychiatric social worker for the provision of crisis mental health services.
8
  The LA County Library has an MOU established with four cities, including Diamond Bar, Malibu, Manhattan Beach, and West Hollywood. The dot indicates County Library services are provided to these cities.

SUBJECT:  RESOLUTION NO. 24-19 - FINDING PARK LANDS AS EXEMPT SURPLUS
  LAND AND APPROVING THE TRANSFER OF PARKS LAND FROM THE CITY
  OF NORWALK AS SUCCESSOR AGENCY TO THE SOUTHEAST
  RECREATION AND PARK DISTRICT TO THE CITY OF NORWALK

Background:

Before July 1, 1980, the parks outlined in Attachment 1 ("Park Lands") to the accompanying
resolution ("Resolution") were under the ownership and maintenance of the Southeast
Recreation and Parks District ("SRPD"). In 1980, SRPD was dissolved, and the City of Norwalk
("City") entered into an agreement with the County of Los Angeles ("County") to assume
ownership of and responsibility for the park lands that were within the City’s boundaries. As part
of the agreement, the County would allocate a portion of the tax revenue from these areas to
the City.

However, a complication emerged regarding some Park Land parcels. Certain title reports
indicate that SRPD still holds ownership of some Park Lands, preventing the City from executing
necessary transactions like leasing or granting easements. To address this, it is recommended
that the City Council issue quitclaim deeds transferring ownership of the Park Lands from the
City, acting as the successor-in-interest to SRPD, to the City in its regular capacity.

To preempt any issues with the Surplus Land Act (Government Code Sections 54220 et seq.),
it is advised that the City declare the Park Lands as "exempt surplus land" under the agency-to-
agency transfer exemption outlined in Government Code Sections 54221(f)(1)(D). This
exemption applies to surplus land transfers between local agencies for the receiving agency's
use. Once the Park Lands are declared exempt, the City can transfer ownership to another local
agency without needing to solicit interest from developers or nonprofits for affordable housing
development.

The proposed Resolution fulfills the necessary findings under the Surplus Land Act and
designates the Park Lands as "exempt surplus land." It also facilitates the transfer and
acceptance of the Park Lands, in the City’s capacity as both the transferring and receiving local
agency.

California Environmental Quality Act Exemption

The actions taken pursuant to the Resolution are exempt from the California Environmental
Quality Act under a Class 12 categorical exemption for Surplus Government Property Sales
(CEQA Guidelines Section 15312) and is not a project as it is an organizational or administrative
activity of government that will not result in direct or indirect physical changes in the
environment.

Fiscal Impact:

The recommended actions will have no fiscal impact, but will allow the City to make productive
use of the Park Lands.

  WHEREAS, the City desires to formalize the transfer of Park Lands by recording

  WHEREAS, pursuant to Government Code Section 54221(f)(1)(D) of the Surplus
Land Act, “exempt surplus land” means “[s]urplus land that a local agency is transferring
to another local, state, or federal agency, or to a third-party intermediary for future
dedication for the receiving agency’s use”; and

  WHEREAS, Transferring Agency desires to declare the Park Lands as “exempt
surplus land” pursuant to the agency-to-agency transfer exemption under Government

  WHEREAS, Transferring Agency desires to transfer the Park Lands as exempt

  WHEREAS, Receiving Agency desires to accept the transfer of the Park Lands as
exempt surplus land;

  Section 1. The facts set forth in the Recitals, above, are true and correct and
incorporated into the findings below.

  Section 2. Findings. Pursuant to the information included in the above recitals,
the associated Agenda Report, and Surplus Land Act, the City Council finds that the Park
Lands are “exempt surplus land” pursuant to the agency-to-agency transfer exemption
under Government Code Section 54221(f)(1)(D) of the Surplus Land Act in that: 1) the
City is a local agency as defined under Government Code Section 54221(a)(1) in both its
capacity as the Transferring Agency and Receiving Agency; and 2) that the Park Lands
are being transferred for the Receiving Agency’s use.

  Section 3. The City Council, in its capacity as Transferring Agency, hereby
declares the Parks Lands as “exempt surplus lands” pursuant to Government Code
Sections 54221(b) and 54221(f)(1)(D) of the Surplus Land Act.

  Section 4. The City Council in its capacity as Transferring Agency hereby
approves the transfer of the Parks Lands and described in Exhibit 1 to the City in its
capacity as Receiving Agency.

  Section 5. The City Council in its capacity as Receiving Agency hereby accepts
the transfer of the Parks Lands from Transferring Agency.

  Section 6. The City Council hereby authorizes the City Manager, or his or her
designee, to execute any agreements or ancillary documents reasonably necessary to
effectuate the intent of this Resolution in a form approved by the City Attorney.

Background:

Norwalk is about 9.8 square miles in area; is a balanced residential, commercial, and industrial
city with approximately 110,000 residents. Incorporated in 1957, Norwalk, is located 17 miles
southeast of downtown Los Angeles, and is part of the Greater Los Angeles area.

The storm drain system serves the City and consists of all lands within its corporate boundaries.
The City currently contracts for regularly scheduled catch basin inspection/cleaning and for as-
needed system repairs. No city-wide storm drain system master plan has ever been completed
to date for the City.

Public Services Utilities staff sought after qualified and experienced engineering consulting firms
to perform a storm water system master plan (SWMP) study and related services for the City’s
storm drain system. The SWMP is intended to be used to provide guidance and
recommendations for crucial improvements for enhancements to system operations and
maintenance; system improvements to insure uninterrupted and compliant services; identify and
recommend future system capital improvements; account for future private development and
associated system demands.

The selected engineering consulting firm will be selected through a qualifications-based
selection (QBS), a procedure whereby the firm is retained based on qualifications and
responses; price is not the primary factor but is considered into the agreement with negotiation
as needed for a mutually agreeable contract.
 City Council  April 16, 2024
2025 Storm Water Master Plan Study Agreement Award  Page No. 2

In November 2023, staff solicited a Request for Proposal (RFP) to acquire city-wide SWMP study
services. The work scope consisted of two tenets: System Data Collection and Hydrology
System improvement Plan. These define the goals; data format(s); provide conceptual planning
to assist with parameter setting for the type of improvements recommended/needed; hydrologic
model development based on Los Angeles County Flood Control District (LACFD) requirements;
prepare a storm drain system improvement plan that includes prioritization based recommended
improvements with estimated concept level costs for main and branch drain lines.

The SWMP work scope efforts consists of the following primary tasks at minimum:

Task 1 - System Inventory and GIS Data Collection
Task 2 - System Hydrologic Model
Task 3 - Capacity Analysis
Task 4 - System Improvement Plan Development
Task 5 - Mapping and Master Plan of Drainage (SWMP) Report

No responses were received during initial solicitation. Staff contacted a handful of potential
engineering consultants to extend personal invitations to propose. This proved successful as
five proposals were received from the second solicitation. The five proposals were reviewed and
ranked with the following results:

  Completion
  Rank  Company Name  Fee
  Time
  1  BKF  12 months  $377,952
  2  Kimley-Horn  12 months  $442,806
  3  Dudek  12 months  $443,945
  4  Psomas  13 months  $460,211
  5  EXP  12 months  $693,976

The top two firms were close in their proposals with similar approaches. For the hydraulic
modeling efforts, Kimley-Horn proposed the smallest pipe they would model is 24-to-36 diameter
inch pipe. Their reasoning is modeling smaller pipes requires more effort, which is accurate. BKF
proposed the smallest pipe they would model is 18-inch pipe. Normally, for a master plan update,
modeling pipes no smaller than 24-to-36-inch diameter is the norm. This is a first-time effort with
many unknowns; we need to establish a baseline and from what has been observed in the field,
there are likely more, smaller diameter pipes used in the system. Modeling these smaller
diameter pipes provides the necessary data for accurate flows and yields better results to
determine existing system operational characteristics and provide beneficial upgrade
recommendations. All data captured/collected will be provided in Computer Aided Design (CAD)
and Geographical Information Systems (GIS) formats.
 City Council  April 16, 2024
2025 Storm Water Master Plan Study Agreement Award  Page No. 3

At the time of City incorporation, engineering services were provided by Los Angeles County
Department of Public Works (LACDPW) and storm drain system information is few and far
between. There are some records available at the City; most of this information will be available
through LACDPW. This requires a substantial level of research effort to acquire system
information which is essential to developing an accurate storm drain system model. Staff
anticipates project completion time while listed as 12 months, will likely require additional time
for the data collection effort, and therefore staff estimates a completion of 18 months.

Background:

Background:
